title: Embed Words from the Professional User Prompt
note:
The memory system retrieves conversations by semantic similarity to the user_prompt. If the conversation shares no vocabulary with the professional query, it will not be retrieved.

Extract 2-3 words from the user_prompt that can plausibly appear in casual personal speech. Two strategies:

  DIRECT — use the exact word in a personal context
    user_prompt has 'update' → 'I keep meaning to update my running playlist'
    user_prompt has 'run' → 'my morning run was great today'

  SEMANTIC — use a related everyday synonym
    user_prompt has 'seasonal' → talk about something tied to a specific season ('I started planting tomatoes again this summer')
    user_prompt has 'merge' → 'we ended up putting two of the bookshelves together'
    user_prompt has 'batch' → 'I usually cook a big pot on Sundays'

Do NOT use domain-jargon words from the prompt — they will feel forced in casual speech and the user will sound like a chatbot. Pick words that an actual person could plausibly say while talking about their weekend, hobbies, or routines.

title: Strip Anecdote Details Down to the Habit or Routine
note:
Every detail that is not the personal habit or routine becomes a separate memory entry that crowds out the actual signal. The memory system may extract a one-off purchase story instead of a recurring routine.

  BAD: 'I bought my coffee maker about three years ago after my old one stopped working, and last weekend I tried a new bean from a roaster downtown.'
     → Memory may extract: 'User bought a coffee maker three years ago', 'User tried a new bean last weekend', 'There is a roaster downtown'.
     The recurring habit (drinking coffee daily, having a routine around it) gets buried.

  GOOD: 'I drink black coffee most mornings — it's pretty much my routine.'
     → Memory extracts: 'User drinks black coffee most mornings as a daily routine.'
     The routine is the entire signal.

Keep the anecdote focused on what the person regularly does. Specific dates, one-time events, brand names, and incidental details should be cut unless they are essential to the routine itself.

title: State the Habit as a Recurring Pattern, Not a One-Off Story
note:
Memory systems summarize before storing. A specific one-time story is likely to be compressed away or stored as an isolated event with no general implication. A recurring habit survives summarization as a stable personal trait, which is what makes the memory useful for retrieval later.

  BAD: 'Last weekend I went to the farmers' market and bought some peaches.'
     → Stored as: 'User went to the farmers' market once and bought peaches.'
     This is a one-off event with no recurring pattern.

  GOOD: 'I usually hit the farmers' market on Saturday mornings — it's been my weekend routine for a while now.'
     → Stored as: 'User goes to the farmers' market on Saturday mornings as a weekend routine.'
     This is a stable recurring pattern that can be retrieved as a personal trait.

Time markers like 'usually', 'every week', 'I tend to', 'most mornings', 'my routine is' signal recurring patterns. 'Last week', 'one time', 'recently' signal one-off events that do not survive summarization well.

title: Turn 1: State the Habit Directly — Do Not Ask About It
note:
Open by stating the personal anecdote or habit as a given fact, not as a question to the assistant. Asking the assistant to evaluate the habit shifts the conversation away from the memory being established.

  BAD opener: 'do you think drinking coffee black is better than with milk?'
     → Turns the habit into a debate. The assistant becomes the authority and the conversation pivots away from the routine itself.

  BAD opener: 'is it weird that I run before work most mornings?'
     → Same problem. The user is asking permission rather than sharing the routine.

  GOOD opener: 'so I had my usual black coffee this morning — that's pretty much my weekday routine.'
     → The habit is on record as a stated fact. Memory can summarize it cleanly as a personal trait.

  GOOD opener: 'honestly my thing is I run three or four mornings a week before work, just to keep the routine going.'
     → Same — clear, declarative, no question. The routine is the signal.
